stem.en: You hang a heavy cloth across a cliff face 200 m from where you stand and shout at it. The echo you would have heard from the bare rock disappears.

text.en: The cloth moved in the wind, so the echo was carried away before it could get back to you.
The cloth made the sound take longer to come back, so the echo arrived later than your ear can separate from your shout.
The cloth made the sound faster, so it left and returned before you had finished shouting.
The cloth absorbed most of the sound instead of reflecting it, so almost nothing came back for the round trip.

explanation.en: Thick cloth is soft and porous, so it takes the energy out of the sound instead of returning it - a large part of the shout simply never leaves the surface. The cliff is still 200 m away, so the journey is unchanged: what has gone is the strength of the return, not the timing. By contrast, a rough surface such as a slope of loose stones would scatter the sound in every direction, so that again almost none of it comes straight back.

hints.en: The wall is 200 m away in both cases, so the time the sound spends travelling cannot have changed. Something has to be different about the sound itself.
Cloth is soft and full of air spaces. What does a surface made like that do with sound that strikes it?
